extracted.intended_audience: trade policymakers, tribunal officials, trade lawyers, and scholars interested in Canadian anti-dumping law and procedure
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing institutional, procedural, and substantive standards for how Canada's Anti-dumping Tribunal and National Revenue investigate, determine, and remedy dumping and injury, including appellate routes and compliance with the GATT Anti-dumping Code. Includes recommendations on institutional design and alternative remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final determination limits and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deputy Minister makes a final determination of dumping, assesses anti-dumping duties on the basis of the final determination, and refunds any over-payment of provisional duty. The amount of anti-dumping duty applicable by virtue of the final determination to goods entered provisionally may not exceed the provisional duty paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values determined at final determination are used to appraise goods entered subsequent to the Tribunal's injury finding; the final determination may be appealed to the Tariff Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redetermination / reappraisal and appeal avenues
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 provides for a redetermination of description or reappraisal of normal value by a Dominion customs appraiser; an appeal from a Dominion customs appraiser's decision to the Deputy Minister; and redetermination or reappraisal on the initiative of the Deputy Minister.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations of the Deputy Minister may be appealed to the Tariff Board, and questions of law are appealable from the Tariff Board to the Federal Court (sections 19-20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic reinvestigation of normal values and export prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Special Assessment Programs reinvestigates normal values and export prices about once a year so that these values reflect changes in expenses, costs and market conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular reinvestigation is used to keep appraisals up to date for goods entered after positive injury findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic effectiveness and revenue impact of anti-dumping duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-dumping duties are unlikely to generate much revenue because exporters faced with duties will raise price to a non-dumped level and thus reduce or eliminate provisional-duty collections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This observation bears on whether duties achieve intended fiscal or corrective objectives and on policy choices between duties, subsidies, or tariff adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional division of functions (investigation vs injury)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an irrational dichotomy of functions: National Revenue is responsible for investigating dumping, and the Tribunal for consideration of injury. This division is inefficient and can cause duplication of effort and fragmentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include duplication in research, inability of one body to benefit from the other's efforts, fragmentation impeding a full grasp of the dumping problem, and awkward appeals split between agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous investigation of dumping and injury (Article 5(b) compliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The divided jurisdiction does not permit what the Code contemplates in Article 5(b), a simultaneous investigation of dumping and injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms are sometimes adhered to only nominally (talking of a 'preliminary' determination while pretending dumping is still being considered), which undermines the Code's simultaneous-investigation requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and case-flow management (Tribunal 90-day limit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal's ninety-day time limit is manageable only if the flow of preliminary determinations from National Revenue is reasonably paced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordination (e.g., spacing preliminary determinations at fortnightly intervals) and case-tracking by the Tribunal Secretary are necessary to avoid overload and to keep hearings within statutory time-limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, secrecy, and reviewability of National Revenue procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms of Special Assessment Programs include excessive secrecy and that Revenue Canada's anti-dumping activities are not subject to review, which some say has permitted abuse of procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An objective assessment would require careful study of Special Assessment Programs' work, which Revenue Canada may not permit; lack of transparency is a recurring concern that limits external evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ministerial prescriptions vs statutory provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Special Assessment Programs has been criticized for resorting too easily to section 11 of the Act (ministerial prescriptions), simply because that is easier than applying sections 9 and 10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-reliance on ministerial prescriptions can be seen as procedural shortcutting and may invite criticisms about legality and arbitrariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological soundness in calculating margins and normal value
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms include calculating the margin of dumping on the basis of the difference between the dumped price and that charged by the Canadian industry (because foreign domestic price is hard to ascertain) and of calculating 'normal value' in an unreasonable or careless way, producing absurd preliminary margins later adjusted in final determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper adherence to methodological norms for determining normal value and margins (including seeking foreign domestic price where appropriate) is required to avoid inaccurate preliminary findings and international criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias and impartiality concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Special Assessment Programs has been accused of being hopelessly biased in favour of Canadian producers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A review of procedures may or may not support these allegations; observable patterns (e.g., frequent international criticism focused on Revenue Canada's methods) warrant careful scrutiny to ensure impartial administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural formality vs efficiency and cost of proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribunal proceedings are criticized as being formal to the point of cumbersomeness, too long and expensive (substantial legal fees; executives away from business), permitting harassment of witnesses and irrelevant cross-examination, and enabling 'commercial fishing expeditions' by lawyers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a basic dilemma: court-like constraints appropriate to quasi-judicial bodies may be mismatched to the Tribunal's narrow economic inquiry, raising questions about whether such trappings are necessary or worthwhile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural flexibility and informality (participant roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: In several respects Tribunal practices are relatively informal: participants can help determine points at the preliminary sitting; members may visit factories unaccompanied by opposing parties; hearings may reopen arguments if later evidence suggests it is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such informality can improve fact-finding and responsiveness but must be balanced against natural justice and appeal risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of quasi-judicial procedures for economic inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: The constraints applied by the courts are those appropriate to a quasi-judicial body, yet the Tribunal is investigating a causal relationship between dumping and injury — a narrow economic inquiry — calling into question whether quasi-judicial trappings are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative procedural models (e.g., administrative inquiries) may be more suitable; statutory change may be required to implement alternatives without exposing the Tribunal to Federal Court oversight issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder representation and participation (consumers, unions, press)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers, unions, and the press have shown limited interest in Tribunal work; consumer associations seldom appear, and unions rarely participate or sometimes undermine complainants by criticizing management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater representation (e.g., consumer associations bringing 'other factors' to explain injury) could help present broader interests, but historically these voices are minimal and press attention is sparse outside sensational events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with GATT / Anti-dumping Code provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The GATT Committee on Anti-dumping Practices has repeatedly criticized Canada for methods of calculation of margins of dumping, determinations of normal value not in accordance with Articles 2(d) and (f), and failure to determine injury per Article 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International scrutiny emphasizes the need for domestic procedures and computations to align with Code Articles to avoid disputes and diplomatic criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of agency functions and potential restructuring
rubrics_metrics.description: There have been proposals to reallocate agency functions: concentrating all appeal functions in one agency and all economic inquiry functions in another; or uniting anti-dumping functions by transferring investigative tasks from National Revenue to the Tribunal (renamed Anti-dumping Office).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such restructuring would require statutory changes and possibly new agencies; considerations include efficiency, independence, and clarity of jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative remedies and discretionary powers (price undertakings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal (or Office) might benefit from weapons other than anti-dumping duties, such as authority to negotiate voluntary price undertakings, which offer speed and low cost though with potential drawbacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Price undertakings can be structured equitably and publicly; drawback noted that undertakings may transfer benefits to the foreign seller by raising landed cost before duty, but exporters often raise prices anyway after duties, producing similar effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy-level reappraisal of anti-dumping as a trade mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Those responsible for Canada's international trade negotiations should consider whether the anti-dumping systems required by the GATT and the Code are compatible with international trade goals or Canada's goals — 'Is anti-dumping really necessary?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives (temporary conventional duty increases, producer subsidies) may be more efficient; a reappraisal should weigh economic efficiency, distributional effects, and international obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional effects: consumer sacrifice vs producer protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-dumping duties tend to sacrifice consumers in the interests of producers; the gross loss to consumers is likely larger than producer gains, suggesting inefficiency compared to alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts (e.g., Hindley, Lloyd) argue for considering subsidies or temporary conventional tariff increases to achieve protection with potentially lower welfare loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for empirical external study of Special Assessment Programs
rubrics_metrics.description: An objective and complete assessment of criticisms of Revenue Canada could only be made following very careful study of the work of Special Assessment Programs, a study that Revenue Canada is not prepared to allow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of access prevents independent validation of procedural criticisms; transparency and external review mechanisms are thus implied desiderata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination of research to avoid duplication and improve preparedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribunal research staff, faced with tight deadlines after preliminary determinations, often lack product knowledge; planning to begin study of a product whenever an investigation by the Deputy Minister is underway would improve preparedness and reduce duplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinated early study by both Revenue and Tribunal staff can avoid two contemporaneous but separate studies and improve efficiency of the overall process.
